title: Top-level sections Part 1
thesis: This opening cluster establishes an audit framework rather than a finished theory: before evaluating any consciousness theory, future episodes should ask what target it explains, what evidence supports it, what relation it claims between brain or function and experience, and what metaphysical commitments it assumes. Its strongest pressure is that explaining function, report, attention, and behavior may still leave the felt character of experience unresolved; its main limits are contested hard-problem intuitions, measurement difficulties, correlate-cause confusions, taxonomic bias, and worldview labels that can substitute for explanation.

durable_concepts.summary: Chalmers's hard problem is the central opening challenge: even a complete account of discrimination, attention, report, memory, integration, wakefulness, and behavioral control may not explain why any of those processes are accompanied by subjective experience. The dossier treats this as a challenge to reductive physicalism, not as a proof that physicalism is false.

durable_concepts.concept: Phenomenal consciousness as a distinct target
durable_concepts.summary: Phenomenal consciousness means what experience is like from the inside, such as seeing red, hearing music, feeling pain, or having a point of view. The dossier distinguishes this from access, report, wakefulness, metacognition, attention, and behavioral control so later theories do not claim success on one target while answering another.

Kuhn's initial framing treats consciousness as a suitcase term that can bundle wakefulness, responsiveness, perceptual awareness, reportability, access, self-awareness, metacognition, emotion, and phenomenal experience. Future episodes should keep the target explicit instead of searching for a single undifferentiated mechanism.

Scientific theories often focus on access, global availability, confidence monitoring, report, attention, and behavioral control because these can be operationalized. That tractability is valuable, but it may leave the phenomenal target partly or wholly untouched unless the theory explains why those functions amount to felt experience.

durable_concepts.concept: Neural correlates require an inference bridge
durable_concepts.summary: The neural-correlates program makes consciousness empirically tractable, but a correlate may be a prerequisite, consequence, report-related process, attentional demand, memory demand, common effect, causal basis, realizer, or constitutive basis. Later episodes should specify which relation is being claimed.

Surveys and taxonomies are needed because theories differ by explanandum, ontology, method, evidence, and testability. They help compare theories and expose assumptions, but they are not themselves theories and can inherit the priorities of their organizing questions.

Physicalism, dualism, idealism, and related hybrids frame the same facts differently. The dossier presents worldview commitments as a compass for later comparison, not as settled conclusions: physicalism has scientific foothold, dualism preserves explanatory pressure from subjectivity, and idealism stresses the epistemic priority of experience.

recurring_distinctions: Phenomenal consciousness versus access consciousness, reportability, wakefulness, metacognition, emotion, and behavioral control.
Easy problems of function and mechanism versus the hard problem of why those functions are accompanied by subjective experience.
Epistemology, or how consciousness is known and measured, versus ontology, or what consciousness is.
Correlation versus causation, constitution, identity, realization, grounding, common-cause dependence, and explanation.
Conceptual or conceivability arguments versus empirical evidence and operational measurement.
A theory of consciousness versus a survey, taxonomy, map, typology, or comparison database.
Worldview labels such as physicalism, dualism, and idealism versus detailed explanatory work.
Conceivability of survival, zombies, uploads, or nonphysical mentality versus evidential support for those claims.
do_not_reexplain: Do not restart Chalmers's hard/easy problem distinction from scratch; future episodes can cite this capsule and briefly remind listeners of the distinction.
Do not reintroduce the basic warning that consciousness is not one simple target; instead, state the relevant target for the theory under discussion.
Do not re-explain the phenomenal/access distinction in full unless a later theory depends on a new version of it.
Do not treat neural correlates as self-explanatory; the baseline caution that correlates are not automatically causes or constitutive bases has already been established.
Do not spend future episodes re-justifying why typologies are useful; use them as comparison tools while noting their limits when relevant.
Do not re-litigate basic definitions of physicalism, dualism, and idealism each time; future episodes should focus on what a specific theory adds beyond those worldview labels.
open_tensions: Whether the hard problem identifies a real metaphysical gap or mainly exposes limits in our concepts, imagination, introspection, or current science remains unsettled.
Whether phenomenal consciousness can be cleanly separated from report, function, memory, confidence, action, and attention in a scientifically useful way remains contested.
Whether future neural evidence should be interpreted as correlation, causal support, realization, constitution, identity, grounding, or some other relation remains theory-dependent.
Whether taxonomic proliferation reflects healthy early-stage cartography or weak operational definitions and insufficiently discriminating evidence remains open.
Whether physicalism, dualism, idealism, Russellian monism, panpsychism, or nonreductive physicalism best fits the evidence is underconstrained by this opening cluster.
Whether Chalmers-style nonreductive or fundamental-consciousness proposals can supply independently testable psychophysical laws without epiphenomenalism remains a pressure point.
Whether functional sophistication in AI or functional preservation in uploading would imply phenomenal consciousness is explicitly not settled by this episode.

callbacks.concept: Ask for the target phenomenon first
callbacks.summary: Use this episode as the baseline reminder that later theories must identify whether they explain phenomenal consciousness, access, report, wakefulness, metacognition, self-awareness, emotion, or some other target.

callbacks.concept: Do not let neural correlates do more work than they can bear
callbacks.summary: When later episodes discuss NCCs, lesions, stimulation, anesthesia, no-report paradigms, or adversarial tests, return to this episode's distinction between tracking consciousness and explaining, realizing, constituting, or causing it.

Use this callback when later episodes rely on Kuhn's taxonomy, Chalmers's Type A-F scheme, neurobiological surveys, explanatory profiles, or databases: maps clarify comparison but can build in priorities and should not be treated as neutral discoveries.

callbacks.concept: Worldviews are visible commitments, not shortcuts
callbacks.summary: Later discussions of physicalism, dualism, idealism, Russellian monism, panpsychism, and neutral monism should use this episode's warning that worldview commitments shape what counts as explanation but do not settle the detailed theory comparison.

callbacks.concept: Hard-problem caution for AI and uploading
callbacks.summary: This episode supports only a constraint: if consciousness is defined functionally, AI and uploading questions can be framed in terms of access, report, memory, and metacognition; if the target is phenomenality, functional sophistication alone does not establish felt experience.
